summary:
Mars Explorer is an interactive web application that turns NASA and USGS datasets into a practical tool for exploring Mars and planning terrain-aware routes. Users can navigate a planetary globe or 2D atlas, with detailed CTX and HiRISE imagery appearing automatically where coverage is available.
The application calculates routes using numerical elevation data, accounting for slopes and crater rims. Users can add stops, compare routing strategies, inspect elevation profiles, and overlay geological maps. Plans can be shared through links and QR codes, exported as GeoJSON, or downloaded as reports.
Our project addresses the challenge of making complex planetary data accessible and useful. By bringing imagery, elevation, geology, and route analysis into one workspace, Mars Explorer helps students, researchers, and space enthusiasts investigate the Martian surface and understand how terrain shapes exploration decisions.
details:
Mars Explorer: From Planetary Data to Exploration Decisions
Mars Explorer is a browser-based application that brings Mars imagery, elevation data, geological maps, and terrain-aware route planning into one workspace. Developed for the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge, it helps users move beyond viewing the planet to investigating how its terrain influences exploration.
What it does and how it works
Users explore Mars through an interactive globe or a 2D atlas. The application starts with a Viking global mosaic and automatically switches to more detailed CTX and HiRISE imagery as users zoom into areas with available coverage. Geological overlays provide additional context about the surface.
To create a route, users select start and end coordinates, optionally add intermediate stops, and choose a routing strategy and maximum slope. The backend searches numerical elevation grids using A*-based pathfinding, including bidirectional search for planetary-scale planning.
Planetary routing uses NASA MOLA elevation data at approximately 463-metre north–south spacing. Detailed Jezero planning uses CTX elevation data at 20-metre spacing, with a separate local HiRISE terrain grid at one-metre projected spacing. Route calculations consider terrain slopes, elevation changes, missing data, and conservative crater-rim constraints. Crater floors remain usable rather than treating every crater as a completely blocked area.
Results include route distance, ascent and descent, slope metrics, and an interactive elevation profile. Users can compare strategies, save plans, export GeoJSON, download reports for printing or saving as PDF, and share plans through links and QR codes.
Benefits and intended impact
Mars data are distributed across different missions, archives, formats, and map services. Mars Explorer connects these resources through a common geographic interface, making them easier to investigate without requiring users to operate specialist GIS software.
Our intended impact is educational and exploratory: helping students, space enthusiasts, and researchers understand relationships between Martian terrain, geology, and route choices. It is a research prototype, not a mission-certified navigation system.
Technology and development
The frontend uses TypeScript, React, Three.js, Leaflet, Plotly.js, and CSS with Tailwind tooling. The Python backend uses FastAPI and Uvicorn. Scientific data processing uses NumPy, Rasterio, pyproj, Pyogrio, Shapely, Matplotlib, and Pillow.
Route searches run on the CPU, while the browser uses WebGL to render the globe. Development and testing used ordinary desktop computing hardware; no custom hardware or onboard rover equipment is required. Automated unit, integration, and browser tests check routing, coordinate alignment, exports, responsive layouts, and preservation of the map view during planning.
What makes it creative
The project connects planetary-scale browsing with detailed local investigation in a single workflow. Instead of presenting separate maps and datasets, it lets users move from observing a landscape to comparing terrain-aware routes and exporting their findings.
Our team considered source provenance, Martian coordinate systems, differences between imagery and elevation resolution, real coverage gaps, computational performance, accessibility, and mobile usability. The interface prioritizes the map and working controls rather than decorative dashboards, keeping complex scientific information approachable without inventing terrain or imagery.
